History and Physical (H&P – Detailed)

Consult Summary:
30-year-old active female marathon-in-training presents with 2-week history of progressive right-greater-than-left knee pain and clicking provoked by running; no instability or locking; plan for rest, ice, stronger NSAID, and physiotherapy referral with precautions provided.

History:
• Main complaint: Knee pain (right > left) with audible clicking.  
• Onset/duration: Began ~2 weeks ago after increasing running mileage (currently 7–8 mile runs).  
• Course: Worsening; now limits running and abdominal exercises; pain starts ~20 min into run (~2–3 miles).  
• Provoking factors: Running, knee flexion/extension during gym core work.  
• Relieving factors: Ice therapy (initial swelling subsided).  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Initial mild swelling of right knee after first long run; resolved with ice.  
  – Single episode of tingling in right toes post-run; resolved.  
  – No giving way, locking, or inability to fully flex/extend.  
  – No stair, walking, sitting/standing difficulties; no redness, heat, systemic symptoms.  
• Review of systems (pertinent):  
  – No back pain, no other joint swelling/pain (hands, elbows, wrists, feet).  
  – No calf pain, color change, or persistent lower-leg edema (only mild transient sock indentation).  
  – No GI, respiratory, or constitutional complaints reported.

Past Medical History:
• Hyperopia; LASIK surgery (date not specified).  
• Severe urinary tract infection in past; evaluated for possible kidney stones (no stones confirmed).  
• No chronic illnesses reported.

Medications:
• Ibuprofen 400 mg orally PRN (“dose/route/frequency not fully documented”).  
• Vitamin D (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Melatonin PRN (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Aleve (naproxen) PRN (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Xanax (alprazolam) occasionally for sleep (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Cannabis (smoked joint) occasionally.  
Allergies: Not discussed / none documented.

Social History:
• Highly physically active: marathon training, ice hockey, regular gym sessions.  
• Tobacco: not mentioned.  
• Alcohol: not mentioned.  
• Recreational drug: occasional cannabis use.  
• Living situation/occupation/finance not discussed.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
(Virtual; limited self-reported findings)  
• Appearance: No current knee swelling.  
• Range of motion: Full flexion and extension of right knee without locking.  
• Gait, strength, stability: Not directly assessed via video.  
• Vitals: Not obtained.

Investigations:
• None performed during visit.

Assessment & Plan:

Issue 1: Right knee pain and clicking – likely overuse/patellofemoral or other soft-tissue injury.  
  • Continue ice therapy frequently.  
  • Reduce running intensity/distance; avoid activities provoking pain.  
  • Prescribe stronger oral NSAID (specific agent/dose not documented) to be taken with food; avoid concurrent ibuprofen.  
  • Referral to physiotherapy for detailed assessment, exercise modification, and rehabilitation plan.  
  • Consider in-clinic orthopedic evaluation and imaging (e.g., MRI) if physiotherapy suggests structural injury or if symptoms persist/worsen.

Issue 2: Intermittent toe tingling / transient lower-leg edema.  
  • Monitor; no current concerning features.  
  • Advise to report persistent numbness, color change, swelling, or calf pain.

General Plan / Safety Netting:  
• Return or seek urgent care for persistent swelling, redness, warmth, fever, knee locking, or inability to bear weight.  
• Follow up after physiotherapy assessment or sooner if deterioration occurs.  
• Prescription and referral to be sent electronically to patient’s pharmacy and physiotherapy service, respectively.

Quality checks:

● Missing/expected elements: No allergy information documented; no vitals; no full medication reconciliation (OTC, herbal, contraceptives, etc.); occupation and smoking/alcohol status not clarified.  
● Internal conflicts: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; occasional minor conversational overlaps but clinically adequate.
